newsitem.title: USA: US 97/98 cotton exports may top 7.3 Mln bales--NCC.
newsitem.headline: US 97/98 cotton exports may top 7.3 Mln bales--NCC.

text.p: U.S. cotton exports in 1997/98 could exceed the 7.3 million bales estimated by the Agriculture Department if China is an active importer, a National Cotton Council economist said Tuesday.

"That'll be the real linchpin," economist Mark Lange told reporters at an NCC board meeting. "We'll do better than 7.3 million," if China sticks to its current cotton policies and has a moderate-size crop.
In two of the past three years, Lange said, China has purchased nearly two million bales of U.S. cotton. Sales this marketing year were pegged at 1.8 million bales.
During a presentation to the board, Lange noted USDA projected larger upland cotton plantings, 14.24 million acres, than NCC did, at 13.39 million.
"Many in the industry believe the actual number will fall somewhere in the middle at 13.9-14 million acres," he said. Last year, 14.41 million acres of upland cotton were sown.

The largest decline in cotton sowing, according to USDA and NCC, would be in the Mid-South, where attractive prices could shift some acreage to soybeans. Corn also was expected to take some acreage, although not as much as last year, as a less risky crop than cotton, Lange said.
Lange said the biggest wildcard on 1996/97 U.S. cotton use was the volume of exports, now estimated by USDA at 7.0 million bales. He said the figure might be slightly higher.
Some 1.3 million bales were under USDA loan at present, but loans would soon expire. "Market experts believe one-third of it has been priced" already, Lange said.

"On the other hand, prospects appear dim for significant quantities of early-harvest cotton in the United States, given the lateness of most plantings," he said. "Thus, current loan stocks may be an important bridge to the full availability of the 1997 crop."
